title: Special Relativity & Modern Physics
subject: Relativity
summary: Special relativity (Lorentz transformations, spacetime, four-vectors, E = mc^2) followed by the experimental origins of quantum theory, a first look at wave mechanics, atomic structure and nuclear physics. A bridge from classical mechanics and E&M to the full quantum mechanics course; chemistry hooks include hydrogen spectra, particle in a box, tunnelling, the periodic table and radioactive decay kinetics.

units.title: Special Relativity
units.summary: Einstein's postulates, relativity of simultaneity, time dilation, length contraction, the Lorentz transformation, relativistic Doppler effect, momentum and energy, and four-vector bookkeeping for collisions and decays.

lessons.title: Galilean Relativity, the Ether and the Michelson-Morley Null Result
objectives: Define an event and an inertial frame, and apply the Galilean transformation to show the incompatibility with a constant speed of light.
Describe the Michelson-Morley null result and why it contradicts the ether picture.
demoIdeas: Michelson interferometer in an ether wind: sliders for wind speed v and arm length L, rotate the apparatus and plot the predicted fringe shift 2L v^2/(lambda c^2) against the observed null.
Galilean velocity addition: a light pulse in the ship frame, with a slider for ship speed, showing the speed an Earth observer would measure under Galilean addition versus the constant c.

lessons.title: Einstein's Postulates and the Relativity of Simultaneity
objectives: State Einstein's two postulates and explain which classical assumption (absolute time, Galilean velocity addition) must be dropped.
Use the train-and-lightning thought experiment to show that simultaneity depends on the frame.
demoIdeas: Two observers on a train and platform with lightning strikes at the ends: toggle frames and a speed slider and see which strikes are simultaneous and when each flash reaches each observer.

lessons.title: Time Dilation, the Light Clock and the Lorentz Factor
objectives: Derive time dilation from the light-clock thought experiment, delta t = gamma delta t0, and identify proper time.
Compute gamma for given v and sketch gamma(v), noting the limits v << c and v -> c.
demoIdeas: Light clock animation at adjustable v with side-by-side rest-frame and moving-frame paths, a gamma readout and the tick-time ratio.
Plot gamma(v) with a v/c slider and marked values at 0.1c, 0.5c, 0.9c and 0.99c, showing the v << c and v -> c limits.

lessons.title: Length Contraction and the Cosmic-Ray Muon Puzzle
objectives: Derive length contraction L = L0/gamma from time dilation and identify proper length.
Compute the survival of cosmic-ray muons in the Earth frame and in the muon frame and show that both descriptions agree.
demoIdeas: Muon-decay survival plot in both the Earth frame (time dilated) and the muon frame (atmosphere contracted), with sliders for speed and altitude and the survival fraction agreeing in both.
A rod passing a marker at adjustable speed, drawn in the rod frame and the marker frame, with the length contraction readout.

lessons.title: The Lorentz Transformation and the Invariant Interval
objectives: Write the Lorentz transformation for a boost along x and derive time dilation and length contraction as special cases.
Apply the transformation to events to find coordinates in another frame, and verify the invariance of s^2 = c^2 t^2 - x^2.
demoIdeas: Boost slider that transforms a set of events between frames and highlights the invariant interval c^2 t^2 - x^2 as the coordinates change.
Event pair classifier: drag a second event relative to the first and see timelike, lightlike or spacelike, with the frame in which they coincide in space or in time.

lessons.title: Relativistic Velocity Addition and Rapidity
objectives: Derive and use the relativistic velocity-addition formula, and show that no combination of subluminal velocities exceeds c.
Compute the composition of two collinear boosts using rapidity.
demoIdeas: Chain of boosts: add successive velocities with relativistic and Galilean rules side by side and see the relativistic total saturate below c, with the rapidities adding linearly.

lessons.title: The Relativistic Doppler Effect and Redshift
objectives: Derive the relativistic longitudinal Doppler formula f_obs = f_src sqrt((1-beta)/(1+beta)) for recession and the transverse Doppler shift.
Relate to spectroscopy: compute the redshift z of an object and the speed it implies, and distinguish from cosmological redshift qualitatively.

lectures.title: Lecture 7.1: Introduction to the Doppler Effect

demoIdeas: Source and observer with sliders for speed and direction; show wave fronts, observed frequency from the relativistic and classical formulas, and the redshift z, including the transverse case.

lessons.title: Spacetime Diagrams, Intervals and Causality
objectives: Draw a spacetime diagram with worldlines, light cones and boosted axes, and read off simultaneity and time dilation.
Classify intervals as timelike, lightlike or spacelike and explain causality (which events can influence which).
demoIdeas: Interactive Minkowski diagram: place events, drag the velocity of the second observer, and watch the axes tilt and light cones stay fixed; shade the future, past and elsewhere regions.

lessons.title: Relativistic Momentum, Total Energy and E = mc^2
objectives: Explain why Newtonian momentum conservation fails under boosts, and state the relativistic p = gamma m v.
Derive total energy E = gamma m c^2, rest energy m c^2 and kinetic energy K = (gamma - 1) m c^2, and show the Newtonian limit.
Use E^2 = (pc)^2 + (mc^2)^2 for massive and massless particles.
demoIdeas: Plot K, p and v versus accelerating voltage for an electron comparing Newtonian and relativistic results, with a ratio readout.
Elastic collision of two equal masses viewed from two frames, comparing p = m v and p = gamma m v conservation.

lessons.title: Mass-Energy, Chemical Energy Scales and Accelerated Electrons
objectives: Compute the energy released in mass defects and chemical-scale effects (about 10^-10 relative mass change for 1 eV).
Compute the speed of an electron accelerated through a given voltage.
demoIdeas: Speed and gamma of an electron accelerated through a slider voltage from 1 V to 10 MV, with a logarithmic axis showing v approaching c.

lessons.title: Four-Vectors and Invariant Mass
objectives: Write position and energy-momentum as four-vectors and compute their Lorentz-invariant norms (s^2 and m^2c^2).
Explain why the Compton and photon-absorption processes need relativistic kinematics for the photon.
demoIdeas: Four-vector calculator: enter E and momentum components and a boost velocity; the invariant mass stays constant while the components change.

lessons.title: Relativistic Decays, Collisions and Production Thresholds
objectives: Solve a relativistic collision or decay (e.g. pion decay, particle creation) using four-momentum conservation.
Compute the threshold energy to create a particle in a fixed-target versus a collider setting using the invariant mass.
demoIdeas: Two-body decay calculator drawing the lab-frame momenta and the invariant mass, with sliders for parent speed and masses.
Threshold tool: beam energy slider for fixed-target versus collider setups and the available centre-of-mass energy compared with the threshold for a chosen product.

units.title: Origins of Quantum Theory
units.summary: Blackbody radiation, the photoelectric effect, Compton scattering, the Bohr model and de Broglie matter waves: the experiments that broke classical physics, with every one a staple of spectroscopy.

lessons.title: Blackbody Radiation, Wien's Law and Planck's Quantisation
objectives: Describe the ultraviolet catastrophe and how Planck's quantisation E = n h f of oscillator energies resolves it.
Use Wien's displacement law and the Stefan-Boltzmann law to find the peak wavelength and power of a thermal source.

lectures.title: Lecture 3: Wave-Particle Duality of Light (blackbody radiation and quantisation of light)

demoIdeas: Blackbody curve versus temperature with a T slider, the Rayleigh-Jeans curve diverging, and the Wien peak marked and tracked.

lessons.title: The Photoelectric Effect and the Photon Picture
objectives: Explain the three features of the photoelectric effect that classical waves cannot (threshold, instant emission, KE independent of intensity).
Use Einstein's equation K_max = hf - phi to compute work functions and stopping voltages.

lectures.title: Lecture 3: Wave-Particle Duality of Light (photons and the photoelectric effect)

demoIdeas: Photoelectric cell with sliders for light frequency and intensity and a metal selector; plot the stopping voltage and current and show the threshold frequency.

lessons.title: Compton Scattering and the Momentum of the Photon
objectives: Derive the Compton wavelength shift Delta lambda = (h/m_e c)(1 - cos theta) from energy and momentum conservation, treating the photon as a particle with p = h/lambda.
Explain why the shift is easily measured for X-rays but negligible for visible light, and what the experiment shows about photons.
demoIdeas: Photon-electron collision with sliders for incident wavelength and scattering angle; show the wavelength shift and electron recoil, and how the fractional shift becomes negligible for visible light.

lessons.title: The Bohr Atom and the Hydrogen Spectrum
objectives: State the Bohr postulates and derive the hydrogen energy levels E_n = -13.6 eV/n^2 and orbit radii r_n = n^2 a_0.
Compute the wavelengths of hydrogen spectral lines (Lyman, Balmer, Paschen) from the Rydberg formula.
Explain the successes and failures of the Bohr model (hydrogen spectrum versus multi-electron atoms, fine structure).

readings.title: Bohr's Model of the Hydrogen Atom

demoIdeas: Hydrogen energy-level diagram: click transitions and see photon wavelength, series name and spectral line colour on a spectrum strip.

lessons.title: The de Broglie Wavelength and Electron Diffraction
objectives: Compute the de Broglie wavelength lambda = h/p of electrons, neutrons and molecules, and state when wave effects are observable.
Explain the Davisson-Germer experiment and electron diffraction as evidence for matter waves.

lectures.title: Lecture 4: Wave-Particle Duality of Matter; Schrödinger Equation

demoIdeas: Wavelength calculator for electrons, neutrons and molecules with energy and mass sliders, comparing lambda with slit or lattice spacing to show when diffraction appears.
Electron diffraction from a crystal: voltage slider and Bragg angles where intensity peaks appear.

lessons.title: Standing de Broglie Waves, Bohr Quantisation and the Double Slit
objectives: Explain the Bohr quantisation condition as a standing de Broglie wave on the orbit.
Use the double-slit experiment with single electrons to explain complementarity and why which-path information destroys interference.

lectures.title: Lecture 34: The Wonderful Quantum World - Breakdown of Classical Mechanics

demoIdeas: Single-electron double-slit: accumulate hits one at a time and watch the fringes appear; toggle a which-path detector.
A standing de Broglie wave around a circular Bohr orbit with n slider, showing whole numbers of wavelengths only.

units.title: Introduction to Wave Mechanics
units.summary: The wave function and its probabilistic meaning, the uncertainty principle, the Schroedinger equation, the particle in a box, the harmonic oscillator and tunnelling: a preview of Griffiths-level quantum mechanics.

lessons.title: Born's Interpretation, Normalisation and Expectation Values
objectives: State Born's interpretation |psi|^2 dx as a probability and normalise a given wave function.

Compute probabilities, expectation values and

for simple wave functions.
demoIdeas: Draw a wave function, normalise it with one click, and shade the probability of finding the particle in a chosen interval; show <x> and the probability density.

lessons.title: The Uncertainty Principle, Atomic Stability and Natural Linewidths
objectives: State the Heisenberg relation Delta x Delta p >= hbar/2 and use it for estimates, e.g. confinement energy of an electron in an atom.
Explain the energy-time uncertainty relation and natural linewidths in spectroscopy.
demoIdeas: Gaussian wave packet: width sliders show the position-momentum trade-off and live Delta x Delta p against the hbar/2 bound.
Excited-state lifetime slider and the Lorentzian linewidth it produces in a spectrum.

lessons.title: The Schrodinger Equation, the Particle in a Box and Conjugated Polyenes
objectives: Write the time-independent Schroedinger equation and explain how boundary conditions force quantisation.
Solve the infinite square well: derive E_n = n^2 pi^2 hbar^2/(2 m L^2) and psi_n, and sketch the first few states.
Use the particle-in-a-box model to estimate the visible absorption of a conjugated polyene.

readings.title: The Quantum Particle in a Box

lectures.title: Lecture 5: Operators and the Schrӧdinger Equation

demoIdeas: Potential-well builder (box, parabola, finite well): solve and draw the first n eigenstates and energies.
Conjugated polyene: slider for the number of double bonds filling box levels, showing the HOMO-LUMO gap and predicted absorption wavelength shift.

lessons.title: The Harmonic Oscillator and Molecular Vibration
objectives: State the harmonic-oscillator spectrum E_n = (n + 1/2) hbar omega, the zero-point energy, and the equal spacing of the levels.
Relate the oscillator to molecular vibration: omega = sqrt(k/mu), IR absorption at the level spacing, and the isotope effect on frequency and zero-point energy.

lectures.title: Lecture 8: Quantum Harmonic Oscillator Part I

demoIdeas: Harmonic oscillator levels with sliders for force constant and reduced mass; swap C-H for C-D to see the frequency and zero-point energy change.

lessons.title: Barrier Penetration and the Transmission Probability
objectives: Explain why a particle with E < V0 has non-zero probability beyond a barrier, using the decaying exponential in the forbidden region.
Estimate the transmission probability T ~ exp(-2 kappa a) for a rectangular barrier and see how it depends on mass, width and energy.

readings.title: The Quantum Tunneling of Particles through Potential Barriers

lectures.title: Lecture 12: The Dirac Well and Scattering off the Finite Step

demoIdeas: Wave packet hitting a barrier: sliders for barrier height, width and particle energy show reflected and transmitted parts and the transmission probability T.

lessons.title: Tunnelling in Practice: STM, Alpha Decay and Proton Transfer
objectives: Describe how the tunnelling current in a scanning tunnelling microscope depends exponentially on the gap, and why this gives atomic resolution.
Describe alpha decay and proton tunnelling in chemical reactions (kinetic isotope effects) as applications of barrier penetration.

readings.title: The Quantum Tunneling of Particles through Potential Barriers

demoIdeas: STM line scan: slider for tip-surface gap and a plot of tunnelling current falling exponentially, with a bumpy surface profile traced at constant current.
Proton versus deuteron transmission through the same barrier with mass and width sliders showing the isotope effect.

units.title: Atomic Structure & Spectra
units.summary: The hydrogen atom's quantum numbers and orbitals, orbital and spin magnetic moments, the Pauli exclusion principle and the periodic table, spectra, X-rays and lasers: the physics under general chemistry.

lessons.title: Hydrogen Quantum Numbers, Orbitals and Radial Probability
objectives: State the quantum numbers n, l, m_l, m_s, their allowed values, and count states in each shell (2n^2).
Describe the shapes and radial distributions of s, p and d hydrogen orbitals and where the radial probability peaks.
demoIdeas: Orbital viewer: choose n, l, m and see the probability-density cloud and radial profile, with the quantum-number counts per shell.

lessons.title: Orbital Magnetism, Spin and the Basis of EPR and NMR
objectives: Relate orbital angular momentum and the magnetic moment (Bohr magneton) and describe the Zeeman effect and the Stern-Gerlach experiment.
Explain electron spin as an intrinsic angular momentum with two projections and relate to the basis of EPR/NMR.

readings.title: Orbital Magnetic Dipole Moment of the Electron

demoIdeas: Zeeman level diagram with a magnetic-field slider, and a Stern-Gerlach beam splitting into two spots for spin-1/2.
Spin precession on a Bloch sphere in a field with an adjustable drive frequency, showing resonance at the Larmor frequency (EPR/NMR).

lessons.title: The Pauli Principle, Electron Configurations and Periodic Trends
objectives: State the Pauli exclusion principle and use it with Hund's rule to write ground-state electron configurations up to Z ~ 36.
Explain trends in the periodic table (ionisation energy, atomic radius) with shielding and effective nuclear charge.

readings.title: The Exclusion Principle and the Periodic Table

lectures.title: Lecture 8: The Periodic Table and Periodic Trends

demoIdeas: Periodic-table builder: add electrons shell by shell following Pauli and Hund and see the energy-level diagram fill, with plots of ionisation energy and radius versus Z.

lessons.title: Atomic Spectra, Selection Rules, X-rays and Lasers
objectives: Describe atomic X-ray spectra (characteristic lines, Moseley's law) and emission selection rules Delta l = +/- 1.
Explain the principle of the laser (population inversion, stimulated emission) and give examples used in spectroscopy.
demoIdeas: Laser population simulator: two-, three- and four-level systems with a pump-rate slider showing population inversion and gain.
Moseley plot builder: select elements and see sqrt(f) of K-alpha lines fall on a straight line against Z.

units.title: Nuclear Physics Basics
units.summary: Nuclear structure, binding energy, radioactive decay, fission and fusion; the half-life arithmetic is identical to first-order kinetics, and the energy scale (MeV per nucleon versus eV per bond) puts chemistry in context.

lessons.title: Nuclear Structure and the Binding-Energy Curve
objectives: Describe the nucleus (Z, N, A, isotopes, nuclear radius R = R0 A^(1/3)) and the strong force's short range.
Compute the mass defect and binding energy per nucleon and explain the shape of the binding-energy curve with a maximum near iron.

lectures.title: Lecture 3: Nuclear Mass and Stability, Nuclear Reactions and Notation, Introduction to Cross Section
Lecture 4: Binding Energy, the Semi-Empirical Liquid Drop Nuclear Model, and Mass Parabolas

demoIdeas: Nuclide chart with a binding-energy-per-nucleon curve; click a nuclide to see its mass defect, binding energy and the iron peak.

lessons.title: Decay Modes and the Exponential Decay Law
objectives: Write decay equations for alpha, beta and gamma decay conserving charge, baryon number and energy, and compute decay Q values.
Solve the exponential decay law N = N0 e^(-lambda t), find half-life and activity, and relate to first-order kinetics (14C dating).

lectures.title: Lecture 8: Radioactive Decay — Modes, Energetics, and Trends

demoIdeas: Decay simulator for a population of atoms with a half-life slider, showing N(t) against the exponential and an activity readout; carbon-14 dating mode.

lessons.title: Nuclear Reactions, Q Values and Fission Chain Reactions
objectives: Balance nuclear reactions and compute the Q value from mass differences.
Explain nuclear fission, chain reactions and criticality qualitatively, and estimate energy per fission (~200 MeV).

lectures.title: Lecture 6: The Q-Equation — The Most General Nuclear Reaction

demoIdeas: Chain-reaction simulator with a neutron multiplication factor slider and a moderator/control-rod toggle, showing subcritical, critical and supercritical behaviour.

lessons.title: Fusion, the Coulomb Barrier and Energy Scales
objectives: Explain fusion in stars, the Coulomb barrier and the role of tunnelling, and compare energy per kilogram of fusion fuel with chemical fuels.
Compare the energy scales of chemical (eV), atomic (keV) and nuclear (MeV) processes.

lectures.title: Lecture 31: Nuclear Chemistry and Chemical Kinetics

demoIdeas: Coulomb barrier and tunnelling: sliders for nuclear charges and temperature, showing the barrier, the thermal energy and the Gamow tunnelling window.
